title: Flu Arrives Early in California as Bay Area Becomes First Hot Spot
excerpt: San Francisco reported its first flu death of the 2026–27 season and Santa Clara County hospitalizations ran 11 times higher than the same week last year, as health officials across California urge residents to get vaccinated now.
body:
• The Bay Area is California's current flu hot spot: the state health department's dashboard rates regional test positivity "high" — one step below the maximum — with 1,788 flu hospitalizations statewide as of Sept. 26, more than at this time last year.
  • In Santa Clara County, flu hospitalizations began at the end of August instead of late November, running more than 11 times higher than the same week last year, with high flu levels in all four wastewater sewersheds.
  • San Francisco reported the first flu death of the 2026–27 season — an adult, announced Oct. 1 — and state data showed 34 flu-related deaths so far this season, per KTVU.
  • Get vaccinated now: it takes up to two weeks to build immunity, and experts say shots should ideally happen by the end of October. Flu vaccines are recommended for everyone 6 months and older, can be given with the updated COVID-19 shot, and are often free with insurance.

Flu season has arrived in California three months early — and the Bay Area is its first hot spot. The California Department of Public Health's respiratory virus dashboard shows the region in red, a "high" rating one step below the maximum "very high," with emergency room visits and flu hospitalizations climbing statewide.

In Santa Clara County, flu hospitalizations began at the end of August; last year they began at the end of November and peaked in January. "Reported hospitalizations are more than 11 times higher this year than during the same week last year. As of today, influenza virus levels are high in all four wastewater sewersheds in Santa Clara County," a county health official told KTVU in an email. The county has recorded no flu deaths so far.

Elsewhere the season has already turned deadly. San Francisco's Department of Public Health announced on Oct. 1 that an adult had died of influenza — the city's first flu death of the 2026–27 season. Statewide data showed 34 flu-related deaths so far this season, according to KTVU, while national respiratory virus activity remained low, the CDC said, though cases are increasing.

An unusually early — and unusually western — start

"It's very uncommon to see flu activity rising this early. It's activity that we might normally see more like November or December," Caitlin Rivers, an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told NPR. Test positivity in the West has risen steadily since early September, she said, and flu-related emergency department visits have been climbing for weeks.

The geography is unusual too: flu usually starts in the South and spreads outward, but this year it began in Western states — California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska. The possible driver is a new variant carrying a mutation that appears better at evading existing immunity, particularly among teenagers. Dr. Alex Greninger, a virologist who heads infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington, told NPR his team is seeing as much flu now as it usually would around Christmas.

"This sad news reminds us that respiratory viruses such as flu and COVID should be taken very seriously, especially for people who are at higher risk of getting sick."

— Dr. Susan Philip, San Francisco Health Officer

This season's vaccine was built for the new strains

The strain that drove last winter's rough flu season — the H3N2 subclade K variant — prompted an update to this season's formula. All three components of the 2026–27 U.S. flu vaccines were updated from the previous season, including an H3N2 component addressing subclade K, which spread widely during 2025–26, according to CDC data reported in mid-September.

Almost all samples now circulating in California are influenza A, a type known for rapid mutation and more severe illness in most years, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Most vaccinated people who do get sick experience only mild symptoms, state officials said.

Coverage is low; officials want shots now

Flu vaccine coverage remains thin. The state dashboard puts flu coverage at roughly 10% to 20% for all ages and 20% to 40% for those 65 and older, KTVU reported; updated COVID-19 vaccine coverage in the Bay Area is below 5% for all ages.

California is following guidance released Sept. 4 by the West Coast Health Alliance (California, Oregon, Washington and Hawaii): flu shots for everyone 6 months and older, COVID-19 shots for children 6 to 23 months, adults 65 and older, people with risk factors and pregnant or postpartum people, and RSV protection for babies under 8 months and adults 75 and older.

Federal messaging is thinner. The CDC has not promoted flu shots as usual under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., NPR reported; the agency declined an interview, saying it is "developing a communications strategy" on vaccination. Former CDC immunization director Dr. Demetre Daskalakis called the silence disappointing given flu's toll on children each year.

Uninsured San Francisco residents can ask about free or low-cost vaccines at the health department's AITC Immunization and Travel Clinic at 27 Van Ness Ave. It takes up to two weeks to build immunity, so shots now line up with the CDC's guidance to vaccinate ideally by the end of October.

What to watch

Act fast on treatment: prescription antivirals such as oseltamivir (Tamiflu) and baloxavir (Xofluza) work best when started within 1 to 2 days of symptoms, especially for older adults, young children, pregnant people and those with conditions like asthma, diabetes or heart disease. Health officials also recommend masking in crowded indoor spaces and staying home when sick.

For Bay Area families, the timing matters twice over: Diwali gatherings and fall travel are weeks away, and schools are in full swing — both move people indoors together. The message from health officials is simple: vaccinate now, before the season peaks.
